sections.title: Grapes and what a vine needs
Label terms: origin and grape growing
Pinot Noir
sections.html:
A thin-skinned black grape that only makes good wine in cool to moderate climates. Too much heat and the fresh red fruit turns cooked. It rots easily, so poor vintages are hard.

In the glass

  • Pale to medium colour
  • High acidity, low to medium tannins
  • Red fruit: strawberry, raspberry, red cherry (fresh or cooked, depending on ripeness)
  • Oak should be subtle (smoke, cloves), so older or larger barrels are common
  • The best age into forest floor and mushroom

Burgundy, its home

The best sites face south or south-east on the Côte d'Or, which splits into the Côte de Nuits (north) and Côte de Beaune (south). Quality rises up a ladder:

LevelWhat it means
Bourgogne AOCAnywhere in Burgundy. Light, fresh, drink young.
Villagee.g. Gevrey-Chambertin, Nuits-Saint-Georges (Côte de Nuits); Beaune, Pommard (Côte de Beaune). More intensity.
Premier CruBetter vineyards within a village. Village name plus Premier Cru.
Grand CruThe very best vineyards, with their own appellations. Most concentrated, longest-lived.

Elsewhere: what makes it cool enough

RegionCooling influenceStyle note

sections.title: Merlot
sections.html:
A black grape for moderate and warm climates, with medium acidity and medium tannins. It is often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon to add red fruit and soften tannin, so the wine is ready sooner.

Ripeness changes the style

PickedBodyFlavours
Just ripeLight to mediumRed fruit (strawberry, red plum), green bell pepper
Riper (warm climate, or later picking)Medium to fullCooked black fruit (blackberry, black plum)

Lighter styles don't need oak. Fuller styles gain softness and complexity from it. The best age into dried fruit and tobacco.

Bordeaux

Moderate and rainy (Atlantic). Most wines are blends, and Merlot is the most planted grape. The Gironde splits the region:

  • Right Bank: Saint-Émilion (and the stricter Saint-Émilion Grand Cru) and Pomerol. Merlot dominates. Full body, black fruit, oak, long ageing.
  • Left Bank: Médoc, Graves. Merlot is in the blend but Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads.
  • Bordeaux AOC / Bordeaux Supérieur AOC: from anywhere in Bordeaux, usually Merlot-led. Supérieur has slightly stricter rules.

Elsewhere

RegionNote
South of France (Pays d'Oc)Single-varietal and blends at all quality levels
California, Napa Valley, SonomaFruity to concentrated; often pronounced oak (vanilla, coconut, smoke)
Central Valley, ChileSoft, medium-bodied, high-volume; altitude gives fresher styles
Stellenbosch, South AfricaComplex, age-worthy Bordeaux varieties
Margaret River, AustraliaBlended with Cabernet Sauvignon
Hawke's Bay, NZMost of NZ's Merlot; light to long-lived

sections.title: Cabernet Sauvignon
sections.html:
A thick-skinned black grape that needs a long, warm growing season. In moderate climates only the warmest sites ripen it.

In the glass

  • Deep colour; dry, high acidity, high tannins, medium to full body
  • Black fruit (blackcurrant, black cherry) plus mint or green bell pepper
  • In warm climates the fruit can taste cooked
  • Often oak-aged: oxygen softens tannin, new oak adds smoke, vanilla, cloves
  • Ages for years into dried fruit, earth, forest floor

Bordeaux Left Bank

Gravel soils help: they drain rain fast and release stored heat at night. Cabernet-led blends come from the Médoc and Haut-Médoc (which contains Margaux and Pauillac) and from Graves (which contains Pessac-Léognan). Bordeaux weather varies, so more Merlot goes in when Cabernet struggles.

Label termMeaning
ChâteauMade from the producer's own grapes
Grand Cru Classé / Cru ClasséRanked in a classification; top price, long ageing
Cru BourgeoisMédoc wines outside the classification that may use the term; some very good

Elsewhere

RegionNote

Sonoma (warm inland)Similarly powerful

sections.title: Syrah/Shiraz
sections.html:
Syrah (French) and Shiraz (Australian) are the same thick-skinned black grape. It needs a moderate to warm climate and gives medium to high tannin and acidity. The signature is black fruit with black pepper.

ClimateTypical styleName usually used
Moderate (Northern Rhône)Medium body, fresh black fruit (black cherry, blackberry), herbal notes, black pepperSyrah
Warm (much of Australia)Full body, high alcohol, cooked black fruit, liquoriceShiraz

Outside France and Australia, the name on the label hints at the style. Oak is common (softer tannin, smoke, spice). The best age a decade or more into dried fruit, leather, meat and earth. It is often blended with Grenache in the Southern Rhône.

Northern Rhône

Syrah is the only black grape allowed in its AOC wines. Steep slopes mean hand work and high costs.

  • Côte-Rôtie: far north, very steep. Complex, peppery; some add a little Viognier for floral notes.
  • Hermitage: one steep south-facing hill. High quality.
  • Crozes-Hermitage: larger, flatter area around it. Less intense, cheaper.

Elsewhere

RegionNote
South of France: Minervois, Pays d'OcBlends and single-varietal; ripens reliably
South Eastern AustraliaInexpensive high-volume, warm inland
Barossa ValleyVery old vines: full body, ripe tannin, cooked black fruit, pepper, vanilla, coffee
Hunter ValleyWarm but cloudy: medium body, fresh black fruit; earth and meat with age

sections.title: Chardonnay
sections.html:
A white grape that makes outstanding wine in cool, moderate and warm climates. Climate decides the fruit, body and acidity:

ClimateAcidityBodyFlavours
CoolHighLight to mediumApple, pear, lemon, lime, wet stones
ModerateMedium to highMedium to fullLemon, peach, sometimes melon
WarmMediumFullPeach, pineapple, banana

Winemaking choices (all optional)

  • Malolactic conversion: butter, cream; softens acidity
  • Lees contact: body, bread, biscuit
  • Oak (barrel or cheaper chips/staves): body, smoke, vanilla, coconut
  • Acidification: common in warm climates to balance alcohol and body
  • Unoaked styles may say "unoaked" or "unwooded"

The best age for decades into hazelnut and mushroom.

sections.title: Sauvignon Blanc
sections.html:
An aromatic white grape for cool and moderate climates. Usually dry, light to medium body, high acidity, and best drunk young: even top examples can turn vegetal within a couple of years.

  • Herbaceous: grass, green bell pepper, asparagus; also blossom
  • Fruit by ripeness: apple and gooseberry, wet stones, up to passion fruit
  • Mostly unoaked, as new oak swamps it. "Barrel aged" on the label signals oak
  • Sometimes blended with Semillon

France

AppellationStyle

sections.title: Riesling and German label terms
sections.html:
An aromatic, cold-hardy white grape for cool to moderate climates, with high acidity and pronounced fruit and floral aromas. It is made at every sweetness level, and its acidity balances sweetness.

  • Just ripe: apple, pear, lemon, lime. Extra ripe: peach, apricot, mango, pineapple, even dried fruit
  • Sugar can be concentrated by late harvest, noble rot, or freezing on the vine
  • Off-dry/medium: stop fermentation by removing yeast, or add sterile grape juice (Süssreserve)
  • Fermented in inert vessels to keep its aromas. The best age for decades into honey and petrol

Germany

RegionStyle
MoselFar north. Light body, often medium-sweet, very high acidity. Steep riverside slopes
RheingauSouth-facing slopes on the Rhine. Drier and fuller than Mosel
PfalzSheltered by mountains, sunny. Dry, medium body, like Alsace

German label terms

TermMeaning
LandweinPGI; light, dry to off-dry
QualitätsweinPDO from one of 13 regions
PrädikatsweinPDO with riper grapes from one region; six Prädikat categories
KabinettLightest; green apple, lime, blossom
SpätleseLate harvest; fuller, riper citrus, some peach
AusleseSelected extra-ripe bunches; apricot, mango, dried fruit
Beerenauslese (BA)Botrytis-affected berries; sweet, honey
Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA)Berries dried by botrytis; rarest, most intense
EisweinFrozen on the vine; no botrytis; pure fresh fruit
Trocken / HalbtrockenDry / some sweetness

Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese can be dry. If they are, the higher Prädikat has more alcohol. BA, TBA and Eiswein are always sweet and low in alcohol.

Elsewhere

RegionNote
AlsaceVosges block rain. Dry, pronounced ripe citrus, stone fruit, blossom. Grand Cru sites; Vendanges tardives for late-harvest
Clare Valley, Eden ValleyAltitude makes them moderate. Dry: lime, peach, blossom, petrol

sections.title: Pinot Grigio/Pinot Gris
sections.html:
Pinot Grigio (Italian name) and Pinot Gris (French name) are the same white grape, grown in cool or moderate climates. Vineyard choices create two very different styles:

Light styleRich style
HowHigh yields, picked earlyControlled yields, picked late (extra ripe)
BodyLightMedium to full
AcidityHighMedium
FlavoursSimple apple, lemonLemon, peach, mango, banana, ginger
SweetnessDryDry to medium
AgeingDrink youngCan gain ginger and honey

Both are usually fermented in inert vessels. Outside Italy and France, "Pinot Grigio" on a label usually signals the light style and "Pinot Gris" the richer one.

Italy

  • delle Venezie DOC / Veneto IGT: north-east Italy. High-volume, inexpensive, light, short finish.
  • Friuli-Venezia Giulia: fuller, more complex.

Alsace

Picked extra-ripe: medium to full body, peach, mango, ginger, dry to medium. Best from grand cru sites.

Label termMeaning
Alsace AOCWhole region; labelled by grape
Alsace Grand Cru AOCSteep east/south-east Vosges slopes; only Riesling, Pinot Gris, Gewurztraminer
Vendanges tardives (VT)Alsace-only 'late harvest'; usually medium to sweet
